tier_reason: The README REPL session (BenchmarkTools medians, N=100) prints the benchmark code, Julia 1.8.0-DEV.438 with LLVM 12.0.1 and the i7-1165G7 CPU, but the baseline is closed-source MKL with no MKL or MKL.jl version, and the M1 half prints no versioninfo and does not name its BLAS. That fails the wave-14 A bar (public code, compiler, flags and CPU for both sides). It is a first-party author run from 2021 with no stated mechanism, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README medians (BenchmarkTools, 10000 samples, N=100 random dense matrices, 100 right-hand sides). i7-1165G7 single thread (BLAS.set_num_threads(1); TriangularSolve with Val(false)): rdiv! UpperTriangular 17.916 us vs MKL rdiv!(copyto!(C, A), UpperTriangular(B)) 19.852 us (1.11x, derived from page data); ldiv! LowerTriangular 19.694 us vs MKL ldiv!(C, LowerTriangular(B), A) 21.561 us (1.09x, derived from page data). Multithreaded (JULIA_NUM_THREADS=8; the README sets MKL to min(Threads.nthreads(), num_cores()) threads, which is 4 on this 4-core/8-thread CPU): rdiv! 8.769 us vs 14.163 us (1.62x, derived from page data); ldiv! 9.871 us vs 15.258 us (1.55x, derived from page data). Apple M1 single thread, BLAS not named: rdiv! 21.624 us vs 46.166 us (2.13x, derived from page data); ldiv! 34.375 us vs 49.124 us (1.43x, derived from page data), and a second ldiv! run of 23.875 us against the same 49.124 us baseline (2.06x, derived from page data).
corrections.baseline: Intel MKL (libmkl_rt.so loaded through MKL.jl; MKL version not stated) triangular solve called through Julia LinearAlgebra: rdiv!(copyto!(C, A), UpperTriangular(B)) and the 3-argument ldiv!(C, LowerTriangular(B), A) on the Intel run. The M1 run prints no BLAS configuration or versioninfo, so its BLAS is not named.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.8.0-DEV.438 (commit 88a6376e99, 2021-08-28), libLLVM 12.0.1 ORCJIT with tigerlake target, JULIA_NUM_THREADS=8, no julia command-line options stated (Julia JIT, no compile flags). BLAS.set_num_threads(1) for the single-thread rows and BLAS.set_num_threads(min(Threads.nthreads(), num_cores())) for the multithreaded rows. MKL, MKL.jl and TriangularSolve versions not stated. The M1 run gives no Julia version or versioninfo.
corrections.caveats: Single matrix size (N=100) from a 2021 author REPL session on a Julia 1.8 development build, on a package version that has since been substantially rewritten (August 2026 kernel changes: native left-upper/right-lower kernels, shortened backward-substitution chains, inlined backward panel kernels), with no re-run; the README still ends with a stale line saying only rdiv!/UpperTriangular and ldiv!/LowerTriangular are supported. The baseline is closed-source, hand-tuned MKL (not a C/C++ -O3 build of the same algorithm), its version is not stated, and the M1 rows compare against an unnamed BLAS with no versioninfo. The single-thread Intel advantage is only about 9-11%; the larger multithreaded and M1 gaps are where small-size threading and call overhead matter most. The README's copy-paste script calls BLAS.set_num_threads(Threads.nthreads()) before the single-thread pair, unlike the REPL session it reproduces. The README gives no mechanism, and the baseline timings include LinearAlgebra's copy of A into C, which is equal work because TriangularSolve's 3-argument form also writes out of place. Not a language-level claim: TriangularSolve is a pure-Julia library (no BLAS call in the matrix path) that beats one vendor library at one small size. Source comments claim the vector right-hand-side path beats BLAS trsv by up to 7x below n=256, but no published harness backs that.
corrections.why_faster: Not stated in the README. From src/TriangularSolve.jl: a pure-Julia blocked substitution. The W x W diagonal-block solves are SIMD-register-blocked kernels built on VectorizationBase, the off-diagonal updates are LoopVectorization @turbo loops (nmuladd!) JIT-compiled for the host CPU, block sizes come from the L2 cache size, and the multithreaded path uses Polyester threads capped at min(num_cores, nthreads). MKL's internals are closed, so blaming the 100x100 gap on lower call and threading overhead in MKL is inference, not measurement.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly; the record's '8 threads' was wrong: MKL ran on min(8, num_cores()) = 4 threads on the 4-core i7-1165G7, and the current source caps TriangularSolve at the same count (the 2021 code was not checked). Downgraded A to C because the baseline side (closed MKL, no version; M1 BLAS unnamed) does not meet the wave-14 both-sides A bar and no mechanism is stated. Under the older wave-8 reading (Octavian.jl, also MKL with no version) the Intel half would be A, so the orchestrator may choose that instead. Shortcomings to record: one size (N=100), 2021 dev-build numbers on since-rewritten code, closed vendor baseline with no version, unnamed M1 BLAS, single-thread margin about 10%, no mechanism stated. Metadata (MIT, 12 stars, 4 forks, last commit 2026-08-15, active) checks out; same_algorithm and same_opt_level stay null (MKL internals and build closed).

tier_reason: The first-party README Benchmarks table (M2 MacBook Pro) compares train_gpt2.mojo with llm.c's train_gpt2.c, and both programs are public. The C compiler, flags, the llm.c revision actually built and how the C average was computed are not stated, and the author calls the figures 'a general comparison rather than precise, repeatable metrics', so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table (M2 MacBook Pro, average training-step time, B=4 x T=64 = 256 tokens per step): train_gpt2.mojo 1704 ms (150 tok/s) vs train_gpt2.c with OpenMP at OMP_NUM_THREADS=10 1987 ms (128 tok/s), about 1.17x (derived from page data); train_gpt2.c without OpenMP 7405 ms (34 tok/s). Commit b28eb10 (2026-07-18) replaced an earlier run with OMP_NUM_THREADS=64 (Mojo 1721 ms vs C 1836 ms, about 1.07x, derived from page data). variants.md reports a separate run of the same train_gpt2.mojo at 1716 ms.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Mojo 1.0.0b2 at measurement time: the table was refreshed in commit b28eb10 (2026-07-18), whose pixi.toml pins mojo ==1.0.0b2. The repo moved to Mojo 1.0.0 and max 26.5.0 on 2026-08-13 without re-running the table. Run as 'mojo train_gpt2.mojo', with B=4 and T=64 as compile-time constants. C side: compiler, flags and llm.c revision not stated; OMP_NUM_THREADS=10. llm.c's Makefile at 2d43e5b defaults to clang -Ofast -march=native with -Xclang -fopenmp on macOS, but the README does not say that build was used.
corrections.workload: GPT-2 124M CPU training steps (next_batch, forward, zero_grad, backward, AdamW update; B=4, T=64, steps 0-40, fp32) for train_gpt2.mojo vs llm.c train_gpt2.c on an M2 MacBook Pro. Both programs time the same region per step. Mojo prints a running average that includes step 0; how the C average was computed (train_gpt2.c prints only per-step times) is not stated.
corrections.caveats: The README calls the figures 'a general comparison rather than precise, repeatable metrics'. One machine, no run count, and a 1.17x edge that earlier read 1.07x at a different OpenMP thread count. It ports llm.c train_gpt2.c at 2d43e5b (May 2024); the README notes that upstream llm.c has since added register tiling to its CPU matmul, so the baseline is stale. The C compiler, flags and revision built are not stated (the commit message calls it the 'naive train_gpt2.c'). The numbers were measured on Mojo 1.0.0b2, not the 1.0.0 the repo now pins. A use-after-free in read_to_dtype_pointer (checkpoint loading, outside the timed loop) was fixed on 2026-08-13, after the benchmark. Mojo exposes only B=4-way parallelism in matmul_forward while C's OpenMP spreads B*T=256 rows over 10 threads, so the comparison mixes scheduling and codegen differences. The project's stated aim is matching C, and the gap is within what thread settings changed between runs.
corrections.why_faster: Not stated by the author. From the sources: the Mojo port keeps llm.c's loop nests but hand-vectorises the inner loops with vectorize[SIMD_WIDTH, unroll_factor=4]; matmul dot products reduce each SIMD chunk with reduce_add. It uses Mojo's parallelize over B (=4) for most kernels, over OC for the weight gradient and over 8 chunks for elementwise ops, where train_gpt2.c uses #pragma omp parallel for collapse(2) over B*T and relies on the C compiler to vectorise. B and T are compile-time constants in Mojo. Since Mojo's 4-way matmul_forward beats a 10-thread OpenMP C build, the gap is probably single-thread codegen (explicit SIMD versus whatever the unstated C flags produced; strict-FP float reductions do not vectorise without -Ofast or -ffast-math). That cannot be confirmed without the C build line.

notes: Numbers match the README; metadata (MIT, 383 stars, 17 forks, last commit 2026-10-04, active) checks out, and llm.c is listed (wave 8), so baseline_in_list stays true. Kept at C. Shortcomings to record: C flags, compiler and revision unstated; author disclaims precision; stale May-2024 llm.c baseline that upstream has since optimised; measured on Mojo 1.0.0b2 before the 1.0.0 migration; margin moved from 1.07x (64 OpenMP threads) to 1.17x (10 threads) between runs; no mechanism stated (why_faster filled from reading the source). Not a duplicate: it is a Mojo port, not a wrapper of llm.c. same_algorithm stays true (same loop nests, different SIMD reduction order), same_opt_level stays null.

tier_reason: The README Performance section gives serial and ispc mcycles on three named CPUs with clang 3.5.0/3.4.2. The harness (grav3Daccel/nbody.cpp, nbody_serial.cpp, nbody.ispc) and flags (common.mk: clang++ -O2 -m64; ispc -O2 with sse2/sse4/avx1/avx2 targets) are public. But the ispc version is unstated and the C++ side is not an equivalent build (-O2, no -march, strict FP, double-precision literals, sequential accumulator), so it cannot be A. First-party, so C; D is arguable for the mt1d rows (threads versus one scalar thread).

corrections.baseline: Scalar serial C++ kernel in the same repo (nbody_serial.cpp, same per-interaction kernel body as nbody.ispc), built by common.mk with clang++ -O2 -m64 and no -march or -ffast-math. The README labels it the 'X87' version, but a 64-bit x86 build uses scalar SSE2 by default (not verified by building).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: common.mk: CXX=clang++, CXXFLAGS -O2 -m64 (x86-64) for nbody.cpp and nbody_serial.cpp. ispc -O2 --arch=x86-64 --target=sse2-i32x4,sse4-i32x8,avx1-i32x16,avx2-i32x16 (multi-target, runtime dispatch) for nbody.ispc, plus tasksys.cpp with -lpthread for the mt1d task variant. llvm/clang 3.5.0 (laptop, desktop) and 3.4.2 (server); ispc version not stated. Timing: rdtsc million cycles via timing.h (from ispc); minimum of 4 ispc runs and 2 serial runs by default (nbody.cpp).
corrections.claimed_speedup: README Performance (million cycles, ispc build vs serial C++ build; the README's own ratios): grav3Daccel 6.79x (i5-2467M, AVX, n=10000), 8.01x (Xeon E5-2640, AVX, n=20000), 14.03x (i7-5960X, AVX2, n=50000); vortex3Dvel 7.06x, 8.15x, 10.95x. vortex3Dvel_mt1d (ispc SIMD plus ispc tasks across all cores, against the single-threaded serial vortex3Dvel time) 12.45x, 86.49x, 88.10x. These rows compare a multithreaded build with one scalar thread and are not like for like.
corrections.caveats: The C++ baseline is not an -O3 equivalent of the ispc build. common.mk builds it at -O2 with no -march (generic x86-64, SSE2) and no -ffast-math, while ispc gets explicit AVX/AVX2 targets. The serial loop accumulates in strict sequential order through pointers into the output arrays (tax[i] etc., all float* that may alias the inputs), so clang cannot vectorise it; the ispc version accumulates into lane-private partial sums and calls reduce_add once per target. The unsuffixed literals 0.01 (grav3Daccel) and 1.0 (vortex3Dvel, giving a double-precision divide) promote every C++ interaction to double, whereas ispc treats such literals as float (ispc docs). With the pre-GCC-6 libstdc++ headers of the 2015 systems, sqrt(float) from <math.h> probably also resolved to double sqrt (inference). The mt1d rows add multithreading against one scalar thread. Results are compared only by printing two sample particles; there is no automated check. One run set per machine, cycles not wall time, n differs per machine, 2015-2017 compilers and CPUs, and no ARM numbers despite NEON targets. timing.h, tasksys.cpp and the makefile scheme come from the ispc examples, so this is the same serial-vs-ispc evidence type as the ispc/ispc entry.
corrections.why_faster: Same direct-summation kernel body, but different builds and accumulator structure. ispc compiles it for SSE2/SSE4/AVX/AVX2 with runtime dispatch and accumulates into per-lane partial sums reduced once per target (foreach plus reduce_add). The serial C++ is built with clang++ -O2 -m64 (no -march, no -ffast-math), accumulates sequentially through pointers into the output arrays and promotes each interaction to double through the unsuffixed C++ literals 0.01 and 1.0, which ispc treats as float. The gain is SIMD width plus ispc's float-only, reassociated reduction, not a language property; the mt1d rows add multithreading. From reading common.mk, nbody_serial.cpp, nbody.ispc and docs/ispc.rst; the README states only that ispc vectorises the same code.

notes: Numbers and ratios match the README exactly; metadata (GPL-2.0, 5 stars, 1 fork, 26 commits, last commit 2017-03-21, abandoned) checks out. Corrected compiler_and_flags (the -O2 flags are in common.mk, not unstated), the 'x87' baseline wording, and same_algorithm to false (lane-private partial sums vs a sequential accumulator, plus C++ double literals). Kept at C under the kostya Julia matmul precedent (release C build, unequal FP semantics); D is arguable since the C++ build lacks -march and does double-precision work. The mt1d 86-88x rows are threads versus one thread. It overlaps the wave-13 ispc/ispc entry (same compiler, same serial-vs-ispc harness code taken from ispc's examples), so the orchestrator may record duplicate. Shortcomings to record: -O2 generic-ISA strict-FP C++ baseline, double-precision literals in the C++ kernels, mt1d rows compare threads with one thread, no correctness check, 2015-2017 toolchain, cycles only.
